transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I feel like I’m always on guard and tense, like something bad is about to happen every time I’m out in the neighborhood. An older pastor at my church recently noticed my visible tension and how I've been avoiding certain ministry tasks, and I realized I just can't keep functioning in my calling while feeling constantly on edge like this.
Have you ever experienced or witnessed a deeply distressing or traumatic event in the past that might be linked to this feeling of being constantly on guard?

Yes, about two years and three months ago, I was caught in a drive-by shooting on my block where a teenage boy I knew was shot just feet away from me, and I had to drop to the ground fearing for my life. That night is exactly what keeps me constantly on guard now. Anytime I hear a car backfire or a siren, it pulls me right back to that sidewalk, and it feels like it's happening all over again.
When you avoid going out in your neighborhood, is it mainly because you fear being reminded of the shooting, or are you worried you might have a panic attack and won't be able to escape or get help?

It’s definitely because I’m terrified of being reminded of the shooting and having all those awful memories come rushing back. I plan my entire day to avoid that specific corner and being out after dark so I don't have to face those feelings or constantly scan for danger. It's not really about having a panic attack, but more about trying to keep myself from reliving that night.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were [F43.1, F40.0]. Based on the patient's clarification, their avoidance of going out in the neighborhood is driven entirely by the fear of trauma reminders and reliving the shooting, rather than a fear of panic attacks or inability to escape. This rules out Agoraphobia (F40.0). The patient meets all ICD-10 criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (F43.1), including exposure to a life-threatening trauma, persistent intrusive memories/flashbacks, avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, and marked hyperarousal lasting for over two years, causing significant functional impairment.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (F43.1). They experienced a life-threatening traumatic event (a drive-by shooting) approximately 2 years and 3 months ago. Following the event, the patient developed characteristic symptoms of PTSD, including intrusion symptoms (flashbacks and reliving the event triggered by auditory cues like car backfires or sirens), persistent avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (avoiding the specific corner and being out after dark), and marked hyperarousal (constantly feeling tense, on guard, and scanning for danger). These symptoms have persisted for over two years and cause significant distress and functional impairment in their daily routine and ministry work.
